heading: 5. A second ko after the capture: 215 and 13169
question: At these two leaves White can ignore Black's capture once, and Black needs one more move. Your S[A-1KO+] and S[A-1KO-] count it as an approach, after which White retakes for free. But Black can throw in at A19 instead and take a new ko first, which saves Black one threat. Should the label count the throw-in, S[KO+] and S[KO-], or describe the clean kill, as yours do?

options.label: KO+ and KO-
options.meaning: Count the throw-in. In besogo: no approaches; Black takes first in 215, White in 13169. They give the solver's count: Black needs as many threats as White in 215, and one more in 13169. They also say that White must answer Black's capture at once, which it need not (Diagrams 1 and 8). This is what the checker prints now. No move's grade changes in either problem.

options.label: A-1KO+ and A-1KO-
options.meaning: Your labels, the clean kill. In besogo: "Black needs to do 1 approach move to start a direct ko"; Black takes first in 215, White in 13169. They imply one threat more than the solver's count, which is the count when Black may not throw in at A19 (Diagrams 1 and 7). besogo ranks them below KO+ and KO- for Black, since it compares approaches first. No move's grade changes in either problem.

recommendation: Your A-1KO+ and A-1KO-, with the solver's count beside them as a note, as we proposed for 10005. A strong player calls a ko direct only when the capture must be answered at once. Here White can play elsewhere once, and Black needs one more move before White must answer (Diagrams 1 and 8). That the throw-in makes this move cost no threat is worth a note, but it does not make the ko direct. S[KO+] in 215 would also rank taking the ko first equal to filling E19 first, which gives White no free move (Diagram 13).
text: Your labels describe the clean kill: White plays elsewhere, Black fills an outside liberty, White retakes for free, and Black retakes into a direct ko (Diagrams 5, 6 and 10). Counted that way, Black needs one threat more than White in 215 and two more in 13169. The solver gets the same counts when Black may not play at A19 (Diagrams 1 and 7).

With the throw-in Black does better. After White plays elsewhere, Black throws in at A19, White takes four stones, and Black takes a new ko first, so White needs a threat again (Diagrams 2 and 4, and Diagram 9 in 13169). The throw-in costs Black no threat where the approach costs one: Black needs as many threats as White in 215 and one more in 13169 (Diagrams 1 and 7), one fewer than your labels imply.

The corner after White's capture has the shape of a bent four, but it is not your BENT4. Black must start the ko at once, or White lives (Diagram 3), so the solver calls it a ko. In your BENT4 leaves, leaf 1 of each problem, Black's stones stay in the corner and White cannot settle the shape, so Black starts the ko when it likes, after removing White's threats (Diagrams 11 and 12). The throw-in leads to a second ko, not to a kill.

By your definition the ko at the leaf is an approach ko. White's capture threatens at once (Diagrams 5 and 7), while Black's does not: White can play elsewhere once, and Black needs one more move before it holds a ko that White must answer (Diagrams 1 and 8). The throw-in is the cheapest way to go on, since it costs Black no threat. Where Black fills E19 before taking, as in your leaf 2 of 215, Black's capture threatens at once (Diagram 13): that ko is direct, and S[KO+] fits it.

What the checker prints now: KO+ in 215 and KO- in 13169, the count with the throw-in, and beside them your A-1KO+ and A-1KO- with their counts, as the reading without it. The comparison with your tree is a convention note, not an error. Its explanation calls the corner after the capture a bent four; Diagrams 2 and 3 show that it is a ko Black must start at once. If you choose your labels, it would print them, with the count beside them as a note, as for 10005.

On the site neither choice changes a grade in either problem (table). In both, Black's A19 at move 1 makes your bent four, which besogo ranks above every ko, so Black's C19 in 215 and A18 in 13169 stay wrong under either label. The choice would matter in a problem without such a move: with your labels, filling E19 before taking, as at leaf 2 of 215, ranks above taking without it, as at leaf 5; with S[KO+] at both leaves they would rank equal.

In the wider area, which adds two rings of empty points on 215's open side, three checks of the throw-in in 215 stay undecided within 2,000,000 nodes: the count at the leaf and both checks after White takes four stones (Diagrams 1 and 2). So does the forced-pass check of Diagram 13, and at the leaf the wider search finds a ko but does not decide whether it is a bent four. The other 25 of this section's 30 checks agree there, and none disagrees; 13169 is enclosed, and all its checks agree in both areas.

positions.heading: Problem 215, leaf 5: White can ignore Black's capture once
text: Black 3 has just taken the ko. If White plays elsewhere, Black has two ways on. The throw-in at A19 leads to a new ko that Black takes first, and Black still needs only as many threats as White (Diagrams 2 to 4). Filling an outside liberty instead lets White retake for free, and Black needs one threat more (Diagrams 5 and 6).

diagrams.caption: The tree's line to leaf 5, marked S[A-1KO+], with White to play. Black 3 has just taken the ko by capturing White 2, and White's group has two outside liberties, a and b.
text: Black needs as many ko threats as White; if Black may not play at A19, it needs one more, the count A-1KO+ implies. If White plays elsewhere once, Black still fails against four White threats; if twice, Black wins. So Black needs one more move before its capture threatens anything.

diagrams.caption: If White 4 plays elsewhere, Black 5 throws in at A19, filling its own ko, and White 6 takes four stones. Black has lost nothing: it still needs only as many threats as White.
The corner has the shape of a bent four, but Black must start the ko at once: if Black 7 plays elsewhere, White lives.

The clean kill: White 4 plays elsewhere, Black 5 fills b instead, and White 6 retakes without a threat, since Black 5 captured nothing. White's capture threatens at once, so Black needs a threat to retake: one more than White.
Black 7 retakes after a ko threat elsewhere, and White's group is in atari at a: a direct ko. Black has spent one threat more than White, as A-1KO+ implies.

positions.heading: Problem 13169, leaf 3: the same corner, with White taking first
text: White 2 has just taken the ko, and its capture threatens at once. Black's retake does not: White can play elsewhere once (Diagram 8). Black's throw-in then leads to a new ko that Black takes first (Diagram 9), while filling a lets White retake for free (Diagram 10).

text: Black needs one ko threat more than White; if Black may not play at A19, it needs two more, the count A-1KO- implies. White's capture threatens at once: if Black plays elsewhere, White wins even against four Black threats.

diagrams.caption: Black 3 retakes after a ko threat elsewhere. As in 215, its capture threatens nothing at once: if White plays elsewhere once, Black fails against four White threats, and only if twice does Black win.
